list.listitem: Patients with microscopic colitis (including collagenous and lymphocytic colitis) present with chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, flatulence, urgency, and in some cases weight loss and incontinence. B
Diagnosis is by colonoscopic biopsy. C
The recommended initial treatment is oral budesonide embedded in a gel that dissolves in the distal ileum (Entocort) given in a tapering regimen over 8 weeks. A
Prognosis is generally good; there is no clear association with malignancy, although some patients are also diagnosed with celiac disease. B

background.definition: Microscopic colitis is characterized by chronic watery diarrhea and lymphocytic inflammation in a colon that appears to be grossly normal. Subtypes include collagenous colitis (which includes a thickened subepithelial collagen band) and lymphocytic colitis (no collagen band).

list.listitem: Microscopic colitis: 1.1/100,000/year in 1985 and 19.6/100,000/year in 2001 in Minnesota. This is likely affected by ascertainment bias, with increasing use of endoscopy.
Collagenous colitis: 3.1/100,000/year
Lymphocytic colitis: 5.5/100,000/year
Collagenous and lymphocytic colitis are both more common in women (RR 2-3).
Among patients undergoing diagnostic colonoscopy for irritable bowel symptoms, 2.4% were diagnosed with microscopic colitis.
Microscopic colitis: 103/100,000
Collagenous colitis: 39.3/100,000
Lymphocytic colitis: 63.7/100,000
Unknown.
A large Swedish target trial emulation study found no evidence that ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, ARB, NSAIDs, or statins were associated with incident microscopic colitis.
Data from the Nurses Health Study found an increased risk of microscopic colitis among women with increased exposure to oral contraceptives or menopausal hormones, with a dose response relationship.
In both collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis, the colon appears grossly normal. Microscopically, there is lymphocytic inflammation.
Collagenous colitis is characterized by a thickening of the subepithelial collagen band (typically >10 mm).
Lymphocytic colitis lacks the collagen band.
Patients with collagenous colitis typically present with diarrhea and abdominal pain (73%), flatulence (67%), urgency (65%), weight loss (49%), or incontinence (43%). B
Patients with lymphocytic colitis typically present with diarrhea and abdominal pain (70%), urgency (66%), flatulence (59%), incontinence (59%), and weight loss (48%). B
Diagnosis is by colonoscopic biopsy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Bloody diarrhea, elevated sed rate and CRP, fever, erythema nodosum
Bloody diarrhea, elevated sed rate and CRP, systemic symptoms

list.listitem: Patients with collagenous colitis or lymphocytic colitis typically present with watery diarrhea. It may be worse in the morning and somewhat explosive, but typically the volume is not like that of other diarrheal illnesses.
Diarrhea is not bloody, and systemic symptoms such as fever or myalgias are typically not present.

In one case series, the mean age at presentation was 57 years for collagenous colitis and 65 years for lymphocytic colitis. The ratio of female to male patients was 6.4:1 for collagenous colitis and 3:1 for lymphocytic colitis.

In a series of 37 patients with collagenous colitis, common symptoms included abdominal pain (73%), flatulence (67%), urgency (65%), weight loss (49%), and incontinence (43%). In a series of 44 patients with lymphocytic colitis, common symptoms included abdominal pain (70%), urgency (66%), flatulence (59%), incontinence (59%), and weight loss (48%).
Microscopic colitis is typically diagnosed during evaluation of a patient for chronic diarrhea. If it is clinically suspected, colonoscopy is recommended, with random wall biopsies.

Colonoscopy and barium enema are grossly normal, with only minor abnormalities such as erythema or edema. Biopsy reveals an increase in intraepithelial lymphocytosis (typically >20 lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells). In collagenous colitis, there is an increase in the subepithelial collagen layer more than 10 µm.
Tenascin staining is sensitive (95%) for collagenous colitis that may not meet formal criteria for diagnosis.
Suspect microscopic colitis in patients with chronic, nonbloody diarrhea often accompanied by abdominal pain, flatulence, urgency, and sometimes incontinence.
Diagnosis is by colonoscopy with biopsy; the colon appears grossly normal.
Initial treatment with enteric corticosteroids is effective.

Oral budesonide embedded in a gel that dissolves in the distal ileum (Entocort) given in a tapering regimen over 8 weeks reduces stool frequency in patients with collagenous colitis (clinical response 81% vs 17%; NNT = 2). A
Alternative treatments include oral prednisolone (limited by systemic side effects) and cholestyramine (limited by side effects and less evidence of efficacy). B

Oral budesonide embedded in a gel that dissolves in the distal ileum (Entocort) given in a tapering regimen (9 mg per day for 4 weeks, then 6 mg per day for 2 weeks, followed by 3 mg per day for 2 weeks) reduces stool frequency in patients with collagenous colitis. Based on 3 RCTs with 94 patients, clinical response was 81% versus 17% (NNT = 2). Budesonide 6 mg daily was also effective as maintenance therapy, but another option is to resume budesonide only if symptoms recur, because patients who relapse can be successfully retreated.
A systematic review of 11 RCTs and 24 observational studies found that the clinical remission rate with budesonide as maintenance therapy was 84% (95% CI 60% to 100%).
A qualitative study found support among patients for on-demand use of budesonide, but studies are lacking.
Oral prednisolone was also effective for collagenous colitis but has been less well studied and has more side effects and is therefore not routinely recommended for this indication.
The benefit of bismuth subsalicylate or mesalazine with or without cholestyramine is unclear for both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis.

A small trial compared oral budesonide with mesalamine or placebo for 8 weeks. Budesonide increased the likelihood of clinical remission at week 8 (80% vs 60%, NNT = 5) and that it was superior to mesalamine.

Two RCTs have compared budesonide with placebo. One study of 41 patients showed that budesonide 9 mg per day for 6 weeks was more effective than placebo for active lymphocytic colitis (88% vs 38%, NNT = 2). A second RCT randomized 57 patients (72% female, mean age 59) to budesonide 9 mg once daily, mesalazine 3 grams once daily, or placebo. Oral budesonide but not mesalazine was significantly more effective than placebo.

In an uncontrolled series of 13 patients with lymphocytic colitis, cholestyramine resulted in improved symptoms in 9 patients within 1 week of treatment. However, adding cholestyramine to mesalamine did not confer any benefit.
Mesalamine is of uncertain benefit, but in a small (n = 46) RCT comparing beclometasone dipropionate with mesalazine, remission rates at 8 weeks were similar (84% vs 86%).
The benefit of bismuth subsalicylate is unclear for both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis.
A systematic review of 8 RCTs confirmed that budesonide is safe and effective, but that relapse rates 6 months after discontinuation of therapy are high.
There is no evidence that use of enteric budesonide increases osteoporotic fracture rates, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or glaucoma.

A population registry in Minnesota identified 162 patients with microscopic colitis treated with budesnode. Approximately 80% had a complete initial response, but 63% had recurrence after initial discontinuation and 58% required longterm maintenance therapy.

There are limited data regarding the use of biologic agents for patients with budesonide refractory microscopic colitis, but in uncontrolled case series some patients do have a symptomatic response to monoclonal antibodies such as adlimumab and infliximab.
Bile acid sequestrants are a treatment option for patients not responsive to budesonide, with a 62% response rate in a systematic review of 23 studies.
Probiotics (Lactobacillus acidophilus LA-5 and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12) may be effective in reducing bowel frequency.
In an RCT of 31 patients, Boswellia serrata extract was effective in the per-protocol analysis (NNT = 2) but not in the intention-to-treat analysis.
Perforation of the colon is a rare complication, and is usually associated with colonoscopy or barium enema when reported in the literature. Conservative management initially is an option.

In a 10-year follow-up of 47 patients with collagenous colitis (40 of 47 female, mean age = 68 years, range 41-95 years), 23% had persistent diarrhea, 8% had a reduction in diarrhea frequency of at least 50%, 50% had full resolution of symptoms, and 19% had recurrence of symptoms after initial resolution. B
In a study of 33 patients successfully treated with budesonide (Entocort), 20 had a clinical relapse after a median of 2 weeks, but retreatment with budesonide was usually successful. B

There is no increase in the likelihood of colorectal cancer. A systematic review of 12 studies with 50,795 patients found a lower risk of colorectal adenoma (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.33-0.58) and a lower risk of colorectal cancer (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43-0.89) in patients with microscopic colitis, although heterogeneity was high. No patients in this series of 46 patients followed for 10 years developed malignancy during the 10-year follow-up period. There may be an association with lymphoma, but good studies are lacking. B

There appears to be an association with celiac disease. In one small series of 37 patients with collagenous colitis, 36 underwent upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsy and 8 (23%) had findings consistent with celiac disease. In another series of 15 patients with lymphocytic colitis, 27% had celiac disease; none of 8 patients with collagenous colitis had celiac disease. B

While a cohort study found an increased risk of death in patients with microscopic colitis compared to age and sex matched controls, the difference was small after adjustment for comorbidities and felt to likely be due to unmeasured confounders such as tobacco use.
There is an association between microscopic colitis and acute pancreatitis (HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.30-1.90).

A matched cohort study in Sweden found increased risk of psychiatric disorders in persons with microscopic colitis, including depression and anxiety disorders (HR 1.6, 95% CI 1.4 to 1.7). The same data were used to identify an increased risk of venous thromboembolism as well (aHR 1.21, 95% CI 1.11-1.32).
